questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutional vacuum of a transition
questions.learningObjective: Identify an institutional vacuum and distinguish it from state weakness or collapse
questions.stem: At my astronomy club a member described a country whose old ruler had just been driven out and whose new leaders had not yet built courts, customs houses or a treasury. Which term names that situation?

options.text: State collapse, meaning no organised government survives anywhere inside the country
options.misconception: treats collapse as the same as a gap between institutions

options.text: State weakness, meaning a government exists but cannot pay staff or enforce its own rules
options.misconception: assumes a recognised state is automatically a capable one

options.text: A legitimacy crisis, meaning the people have rejected the rules their government writes
options.misconception: confuses weak institutions with a popular revolt

options.text: An institutional vacuum, meaning institutions have collapsed and no replacements have formed

questions.explanation: A vacuum appears when old institutions collapse before replacements form, leaving authority unclear. Weakness assumes surviving capacity, and collapse implies organised rule has ceased.
questions.hint: Ask what exists between one authority and the next.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement written after the contest
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a negotiated settlement from a truce, capitulation or imposed peace

stimulus.body: Entry for 9 August: I copied out a clause from an old settlement document binding two governments to keep the peace for a stated number of years. It names no conquest and names no future campaign, only terms both sides promised to honour. My neighbour called it a compromise peace.

questions.stem: Judging from the log entry above, which kind of settlement does the entry discuss?

options.text: A punitive peace, arranged mainly to strip the defeated side of territory and resources
options.misconception: assumes every settlement after a contest punishes the loser

options.text: A balance-of-power peace, arranged mainly to freeze the military situation where it stood
options.misconception: confuses a negotiated treaty with a mere pause in fighting

options.text: A unilateral imposition, dictated by the victor alone with no bargaining whatever
options.misconception: treats a signed agreement as written by only one side

options.text: A negotiated compromise peace, arranged on mutual concessions to prevent renewed war

questions.explanation: The entry stresses terms honoured by both governments, the mark of a compromise peace. Punitive or imposed settlements lack mutual bargain, and a frozen military line is not a settlement.
questions.hint: Ask which side had to concede for the agreement to hold.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stages of a European integration project
questions.learningObjective: Order the stages of a European integration project and explain what each added
questions.stem: In my notebook I keep a scheme of how a European economic union developed. Explain the sequence of stages in such an integration project, from the first shared authority through a common market to political union, and say why each stage followed from the one before.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would list the stages in order: first a sectoral community placing one heavy industry under a shared authority, then an economic community building a common market and removing internal customs duties, and finally a political union with common law-making and institutions. It would add that each step widened the areas under shared control, and that the first step was deliberately narrow to win agreement.

questions.explanation: The item tests an ordered account: sectoral authority, then a common market, then political institutions. Answers presenting the stages as simultaneous, or reversing the order, miss the sequence.
questions.hint: Think of the union widening its scope step by step.

questions.topic: A competence held only at the common level
questions.learningObjective: Explain exclusive competences held only at the common level

stimulus.body: Reading note: the union's founding documents listed a handful of matters that only the shared institutions could decide, among them competition rules and the common commercial policy. Everything else was left to national parliaments to settle as they liked. My friend called this the list of exclusive competences.

questions.stem: On the evidence of the reading note above, what does the list of exclusive competences describe?

options.text: Powers that only member governments keep, which the shared institutions may never touch
options.misconception: reads exclusive as meaning reserved to the national level

options.text: Powers shared by every member state, which each national parliament may still override
options.misconception: assumes shared powers stay under national control

options.text: Powers given to the shared institutions alone, with member states barred from exercising them
options.misconception: confuses exclusive common powers with powers kept by members

options.text: Powers held only at the common level, which member states must leave to shared institutions

questions.explanation: The note says only the shared institutions could decide those matters, which is exclusive common competence. Reserved powers and nationally controlled shared powers are different arrangements.
questions.hint: Ask who alone holds the power named in the list.

options.misconception: confuses the common commercial policy with national autonomy

options.text: It places external trade under the shared level, so member states give up separate external tariffs
It guarantees that goods from outside must pay the same tariff in every member state
options.misconception: reads a common external tariff as meaning no tax at all

options.misconception: confuses the internal market with outside goods

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The bargain at a tariff round
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the bargain struck at a tariff round and who gained from it
questions.stem: Between observing runs I wrote about a trade conference where a general rule of reciprocal cuts was exchanged for quicker reductions on a shorter list of goods. Explain how that bargain works and why smaller delegations accepted it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would explain that each delegation agreed to lower its own duties in general, provided all others did the same, so no single industry would bear the whole burden of opening up. In exchange for accepting that general rule, the larger delegations agreed that the sharpest cuts would fall on a shorter list of goods. Both sides therefore traded certainty against speed, and the round became more predictable for business.

questions.explanation: The item tests the exchange at the heart of such a round: a general reciprocal rule traded for faster cuts on a shorter list. One-sided concessions and free-trade ideals miss the bargain.
questions.hint: Think about what each side gave up to get the other side.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A competence held only at the common level
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a member state must not do when a competence is exclusive
questions.stem: In my log I wrote about a matter that only the shared level may decide, and about what member states still keep. Explain what exclusive competence at the common level does and does not allow a member state to do.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that an exclusive competence is one the treaties assign to the union alone, so the shared institutions decide it and member states are bound by the result. It would note that the arrangement concerns the allocation of power, not the level of scrutiny: member states keep their own institutions, courts and parliaments, and they may of course apply the common rule domestically through their own administrations without re-opening the decision.

questions.explanation: The item tests both the limit and the boundary of exclusive competence. Answers describing it as a ban on member states altogether, or as no restriction at all, miss the point.
questions.hint: Ask what member states keep, and what they must not do.

questions.topic: The bargain at a tariff round
questions.learningObjective: Identify the exchange that defines the bargain at a tariff round

stimulus.body: Conference note: I sat in on a session where a chair described how the round was settled. She said the small delegations had wanted every cut to be matched by others, and the large delegations had wanted the sharpest falls to come quickly on a limited list of goods. The chair said the deal gave each side the thing it had wanted most, and that the final package was described as an exchange.

questions.stem: Using the conference note above, which best describes the bargain reached at the round?

options.text: A one-sided concession, in which the large delegations imposed the final list
options.misconception: ignores the matching condition the smaller delegations won

options.text: A reciprocal exchange, in which general cuts were traded for faster reductions on a short list
A complete free-trade agreement, in which every duty was abolished at once
options.misconception: confuses the round with the abolition of all duties

options.text: A frozen tariff list, in which nothing changed but the paperwork was tidied
options.misconception: treats an exchange of reductions as a change of none

questions.explanation: The chair described each side receiving what it wanted most in an exchange, which is the bargain of the round. One-sided imposition, total abolition and a frozen list are all excluded by the note.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutional vacuum of a transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain an institutional vacuum and contrast it with mere state weakness
questions.stem: My log for the winter describes a revolution that removed the old government and left the country without courts, a treasury or a police force for eight months. Explain what a period like this is called and how it differs from mere weakness of government.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would call such a period an institutional vacuum: the institutions through which a state governs had broken down faster than any replacement could be built, so authority, enforcement and collection of taxes all lapsed. It would contrast this with state weakness, where institutions continue to function but lack money or reach, and with state collapse, where organised rule has disappeared altogether rather than being suspended.

questions.explanation: The item tests the distinction between a gap in institutional life and simply weak government. Treating any poorly governed country as a vacuum misses the feature of collapse without replacement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the institutions still functioned at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutional vacuum of a transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a period without functioning institutions is called a vacuum

stimulus.body: Reading note: after the dynastic crisis the council of the realm stopped sitting, the courts closed their doors and the coinage stopped changing hands for two years. The regency that eventually took over issued a proclamation calling that interval a vacuum of institutions, since no lawful body had replaced the ones that stopped working.

questions.stem: The proclamation quoted in the note calls the interval a vacuum because of what?

options.text: Because the regency wanted to excuse its own delay in forming a lawful council
options.misconception: reads the diagnosis as propaganda to cover a slow takeover

options.text: Because no individual had yet been crowned, making the succession legally unclear
options.misconception: confuses a gap in institutions with a gap in a single crown

options.text: Because the state's borders were uncertain and no map of them was recognised
options.misconception: mistakes an institutional gap for a question of borders

options.text: Because institutions had stopped working while no lawful body had taken their place

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stages of a European integration project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stage of an integration project from one distinguishing feature
questions.stem: During a long drive I explained to my nephew why a customs union sits between a free trade area and an economic union. Which description fits the middle stage of the project?

options.text: A customs union, with internal duties removed and a shared barrier against outside goods
options.misconception: confuses a customs union with a free trade area

options.text: A free trade area, with duties removed inside but no shared barrier on outside goods
A political union, with common institutions and law-making already pooled
options.misconception: treats a trade stage as if political pooling had happened

options.text: A currency union, in which members share a currency and a central monetary authority
options.misconception: jumps to a later stage of the sequence

questions.explanation: Internal free trade with no shared external barrier describes a free trade area, the stage before a customs union. A customs union adds the common barrier, and political or currency union come later.
questions.hint: Check whether outside goods face one shared barrier.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the European project
questions.learningObjective: Read an exhibit and identify the order of the integration project

stimulus.body: Exhibit label: the display boards in the county museum showed the growth of a regional union in chronological order. The first board described a shared authority for one heavy industry; the second described a common market for goods between members; the third described a political union with a shared budget and common institutions. Each board was dated later than the one before.

questions.stem: The museum boards I read present which ordering of the European project?

options.text: Shared authority for one industry, then a common market, then a political union with common institutions
A common market, then shared authority for one industry, then a political union with common institutions
options.misconception: puts the trade stage before the shared industrial stage

options.text: A political union with common institutions, then a common market, then shared authority for one industry
options.misconception: reverses the whole sequence described by the boards

options.text: Shared authority for one industry, then a political union with common institutions, then a common market
options.misconception: moves the common market after the political stage

questions.explanation: The boards are dated from shared industrial authority, to a common market, to a political union with a shared budget, each later than the last. The alternatives reorder these dated stages.
questions.hint: Read the boards from the earliest date upwards.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A competence held only at the common level
questions.learningObjective: Define exclusive competence and explain why it is written into the treaties
questions.stem: My notes also describe what the union may not do with other subjects. Explain the idea of exclusive competence and why it is written into the treaties rather than left to custom.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would define exclusive competence as a subject assigned to the union alone, so that the shared institutions decide it and member states are bound and may not legislate on it themselves. It would add that the treaties state the list explicitly so the division of power is certain and identical in every state, rather than resting on shifting political practice that each government could interpret in its own favour.

questions.explanation: The item tests the definition of the idea and the reason for writing it down explicitly. Answers leaving the definition vague, or treating practice as sufficient, miss the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask why a written list beats custom here.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A clause on external trade
questions.learningObjective: Separate the treatment of outside goods from that of goods inside the union
questions.stem: I was asked how a clause on external trade differs from the arrangements among members themselves. Which statement captures the difference correctly?

options.text: The clause ends duties between members, while trade with outside suppliers stays national
options.misconception: reverses which side of trade the clause governs

options.text: The clause keeps external trade national but requires members to consult before changing it
options.misconception: treats a common competence as a consultation duty

options.text: The clause places external trade at the shared level, while internal duties are removed
The clause removes internal duties and leaves external trade to a single fixed rate
options.misconception: adds a fixed rate that no such clause contains

questions.explanation: Such a clause governs dealings with outside suppliers and moves that to the shared level, while duties between members are abolished by the union's rules. The others invert or invent features.
questions.hint: Separate what faces outside goods from what faces inside.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The bargain at a tariff round
questions.learningObjective: Identify the bargain reached at a tariff round from a conference account

stimulus.body: Conference note: I sat in on a session where a chair described how the round was settled. She said the small delegations had wanted every cut to be matched by others, and the large delegations had wanted the sharpest falls to come quickly on a limited list of goods. The chair said the deal gave each side the thing it had wanted most, and that the final package was described as an exchange.

questions.stem: The chair's summary of the round describes which bargain?

options.text: A one-sided concession, in which the large delegations imposed the final list
options.misconception: ignores the matching condition the smaller delegations won

options.text: A reciprocal exchange, in which general cuts were traded for faster reductions on a short list
A complete free-trade agreement, in which every duty was abolished at once
options.misconception: confuses the round with the abolition of all duties

options.text: A frozen tariff list, in which nothing changed but the paperwork was tidied
options.misconception: treats an exchange of reductions as a change of none

questions.explanation: The chair described each side receiving what it wanted most in an exchange, which is the bargain of the round. One-sided imposition, total abolition and a frozen list are all excluded by the note.
questions.hint: Ask what each side obtained in the deal.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Consequences of removing a tariff
questions.learningObjective: Predict the effect of removing a duty on the price paid by buyers
questions.stem: I was discussing with a shopkeeper what would follow if the duty on imported tinned food were removed. Which outcome for the shopkeeper's customers is correct?

options.text: They pay less for tinned goods, because the duty was part of the shelf price
They pay more, because foreign suppliers raise prices once the duty is removed
options.misconception: assumes importers raise prices when a duty is removed

options.text: They pay the same, because removing a duty never changes the final price
options.misconception: believes tax changes never reach the shelf price

options.text: They pay less only for foreign brands, while local brands keep their prices
options.misconception: assumes the duty affected one brand but not another

questions.explanation: A duty on imported goods is normally passed on in the shelf price, so removing it lets importers charge less. Foreign suppliers raising prices, or prices staying put, contradict how the duty worked.
questions.hint: Ask where the duty appeared in the final price.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The institutional vacuum of a transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain the outcome of a collapse of government and how to diagnose it
questions.stem: My log for the spring records the collapse of a military government that left no functioning administration behind. Explain what this produced, and how a historian would distinguish it from a state that merely governs badly.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the collapse produced an institutional vacuum, since the bodies that had collected taxes, heard cases and kept order ceased to operate and no replacement authority took over their functions, leaving power contested. It would contrast this with a badly governed state, where the same institutions continue to function and the complaint concerns their capacity, their fairness or their expense rather than their survival.

questions.explanation: The item tests both the description of the outcome and the diagnostic difference from poor governance. Answers naming the gap but unable to separate it from weak government are incomplete.
questions.hint: Check whether the institutions survived the change.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement written after the contest
questions.learningObjective: Identify the kind of settlement described by its terms and mutual limits

stimulus.body: Reading note: the article on the peace settlement opened by saying that the war had ended and that the document was intended to last. It described terms about the frontier, about prisoners and about property claims, and it noted that the two governments had each accepted limits on their demands so that neither could simply dictate the result.

questions.stem: The article opening on the peace settlement describes what kind of settlement?

options.text: An armistice, in which the document paused the fighting and left terms for later
options.misconception: ignores the note that the settlement was meant to last

options.text: A capitulation, in which one government imposed terms on the other without bargaining
options.misconception: misses the note that each side accepted limits on demands

options.text: A negotiated peace settlement, lasting terms accepted by both governments
A temporary truce, in which the two sides merely agreed to meet again later
options.misconception: reduces a lasting settlement to a promise to reconvene

questions.explanation: The article says the settlement was meant to last, sets out agreed terms and records mutual limits on demands, marking a negotiated peace. An armistice and a loose truce contradict that.
questions.hint: Look for the note that the terms were meant to last.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The stages of a European integration project
questions.learningObjective: Compare the first and last stages of an integration project
questions.stem: I was asked to compare the first stage of a European integration project with the last. Which statement captures the difference most accurately?

options.text: The first stage gave up political power, while the last stage only pooled industrial rules
options.misconception: swaps the content of the first and last stages

options.text: The first stage pooled rules for one industry, while the last pooled institutions and a budget
The first stage created a common market, while the last stage limited tariffs on imports
options.misconception: puts a middle stage at each end of the sequence

options.text: The first stage settled the frontier, while the last stage organised a joint commission
options.misconception: borrows peace-settlement features that belong to no stage

questions.explanation: The project began by pooling rules for one industry and ended with shared institutions and a budget, so the contrast is sectoral control against pooled political power. The others misattach it.
questions.hint: Compare the narrowest stage with the widest.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the European project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the order of the integration project from a narrative ladder

stimulus.body: Entry for 5 February: I explained the growth of the regional union to a visiting student using a simple ladder. The first rung was a shared authority over one heavy industry, the second was a common market with duties removed between members, the third was a political union with common institutions and a shared budget, and the last rung was the currency and the rule-making the member states had kept. The student wrote the rungs down in the order I gave them.

questions.stem: The ladder drawn in my log describes which sequence of stages?

options.text: Shared industrial authority, then a common market, then political union and shared institutions
A common market, then shared industrial authority, then political union with common institutions
options.misconception: puts the trade stage ahead of the industrial stage

options.text: Political union with common institutions, then a common market, then shared industrial authority
options.misconception: reads the ladder from the top rung downwards

options.text: Shared industrial authority, then political union with common institutions, then a common market
options.misconception: swaps the final two rungs of the ladder

questions.explanation: The ladder runs from shared industrial authority, to a common market, to a political union with shared institutions and a budget. Each alternative reverses or shifts the order the student wrote down.
questions.hint: Read the rungs in the order the log gives them.
